June 1, 2026

About This Report

This reproducible analysis report demonstrates the data preparation, variable construction, descriptive statistics, primary analyses, and figures for the study.

Therefore, it illustrates how the analyses were produced from the data set using a transparent, reproducible Quarto workflow, examining experiences in long-distance romantic relationships in relation to attachment styles and prior relationship experience.

Study Overview

This design study examined whether relationship satisfaction varies with communication responsiveness, prior relationship experience, attachment styles, and their interactions.

The design included one manipulated independent variable and two categorical moderators: Communication Responsiveness (High vs. Low) is the independent variable, and Prior Relationship Experience (Prior vs. None) and Attachment Styles (Secure vs. Insecure) are the moderators. While, the dependent variable was relationship satisfaction.

Primary analyses tested whether communication responsiveness, prior relationship experience, and attachment styles and their interaction predicted each outcome.

Setup and Software Environment

This section shows how the packages were installed and downloaded, and how they were used for data preparation, scale construction, statistical modeling, estimation of marginal means, and figure creation.

Load Packages

Show code 
library(tidyverse)  # data manipulation + plotting
library(psych)      # scale construction + reliability
library(afex)       # ANOVA models + effect sizes
library(emmeans)    # estimated marginal means + confidence intervals

Data Source and Long-Distance Romantic Relationship Analysis Dataset

The data set was imported from the Long Distance Final Project folder, and saved as study_raw so that the original file remained unchanged throughout the report.

Along with this, a smaller analysis data set was then created for the current analyses. The data set contained the study condition variables, demographic variables, relationship assessment items, adult assessment items, dependence items, closeness discomfort items, and anxiety items needed for variable preparation and analysis.

Variable Preparation

This section prepares the variables used in the primary analyses, with the original imported dataset remaining unchanged, including the prepared variables created in the dataset, study_data.

Prepare Participant ID and Experimental Condition

Show code 
study_data <- study_data %>%
  mutate(
    id = row_number(),

    condition = factor(
      condition,
      levels = c(0, 1),
      labels = c("Low", "High")
    ),

    relationship_exp = factor(
      relationship_exp,
      levels = c(0, 1),
      labels = c("No", "Yes")
    ),

    gender = factor(
      gender,
      levels = c(1, 2, 3, 4, 5),
      labels = c(
        "Female",
        "Male",
        "Transgender",
        "Prefer not to say",
        "Other"
      )
    )
  )

The experimental condition variables were recoded as a labeled factor for Condition, Relationship Experience, and Gender, resulting in two to five levels for each. Condition and Relationship Experience both have two levels: Low/High and No/Yes. Gender includes five levels: Female, Male, Transgender, Prefer not to say, and Others. As a result, a participant ID variable was created to ensure each row in the analysis dataset had a unique identifier.

Reverse-Code Scale Items

Reverse-Code Scale Items were transformed before Relationship Assessment Scale and Adult Attachment Scale scores were computed. The items used a 1-5 response scale, with reverse coding created by subtracting each original item response from 6.

Show code 
study_data <- study_data %>%
  mutate(
    # Reverse-code RAS items
    # Original scale: 1 to 5
    # Higher recoded scores = higher relationship satisfaction
    RAS4r = 6 - RAS4,
    RAS7r = 6 - RAS7,

    # Reverse-code AAS items
    # Original scale: 1 to 5
    # Higher recoded scores = higher attachment dimension score
    AAS3r  = 6 - AAS3,
    AAS4r  = 6 - AAS4,
    AAS7r  = 6 - AAS7,
    AAS13r = 6 - AAS13,
    AAS14r = 6 - AAS14,
    AAS17r = 6 - AAS17
  )

Create Scale Scores

The reverse-coding scale shows examples of original and reverse-coded items, where the reverse-coded variables were created before the Relationship Assessment Scale and Adult Attachment Scale were computed.

Show code 
ras_items <- c("RAS1", "RAS2", "RAS3", "RAS4r", "RAS5", "RAS6", "RAS7r")

aas_total_items <- c("AAS1", "AAS2", "AAS3r", "AAS4r", "AAS5", 
                     "AAS6", "AAS7r", "AAS8", "AAS9", "AAS10", 
                     "AAS11", "AAS12", "AAS13r", "AAS14r", "AAS15", 
                     "AAS16", "AAS17r", "AAS18")

aas_depend_items <- c("AAS1", "AAS2", "AAS3r", "AAS4r", "AAS5", "AAS6")

aas_anxiety_items <- c("AAS7r", "AAS8", "AAS9", "AAS10", "AAS11", "AAS12")

aas_close_items <- c("AAS13r", "AAS14r", "AAS15", "AAS16", "AAS17r", "AAS18")

study_data <- study_data %>%
  mutate(
    ras_scale = rowMeans(select(., all_of(ras_items)), na.rm = TRUE),
    aas_total_scale = rowMeans(select(., all_of(aas_total_items)), na.rm = TRUE),
    aas_depend_scale = rowMeans(select(., all_of(aas_depend_items)), na.rm = TRUE),
    aas_anxiety_scale = rowMeans(select(., all_of(aas_anxiety_items)), na.rm = TRUE),
    aas_close_scale = rowMeans(select(., all_of(aas_close_items)), na.rm = TRUE)
  )

Create Attachment Groups

Closeness discomfort, dependence, attachment anxiety, and overall attachment group variables were created for the planned 2 x 2 ANOVA models. Participants with attachment scores at or below the sample median were assigned to the Low group, and the participants above the sample median were assigned to the High group.

Show code 
# Create median values for the attachment scale scores
aas_total_median <- median(study_data$aas_total_scale, na.rm = TRUE)
aas_depend_median <- median(study_data$aas_depend_scale, na.rm = TRUE)
aas_anxiety_median <- median(study_data$aas_anxiety_scale, na.rm = TRUE)
aas_close_median <- median(study_data$aas_close_scale, na.rm = TRUE)

# Create median-split attachment groups
study_data <- study_data %>%
  mutate(
    aas_total_group = if_else(
      aas_total_scale <= aas_total_median,
      "Lower attachment insecurity",
      "Higher attachment insecurity"
    ),
    aas_total_group = factor(
      aas_total_group,
      levels = c("Lower attachment insecurity", "Higher attachment insecurity")
    ),

    aas_depend_group = if_else(
      aas_depend_scale <= aas_depend_median,
      "Lower dependence insecurity",
      "Higher dependence insecurity"
    ),
    aas_depend_group = factor(
      aas_depend_group,
      levels = c("Lower dependence insecurity", "Higher dependence insecurity")
    ),

    aas_anxiety_group = if_else(
      aas_anxiety_scale <= aas_anxiety_median,
      "Lower attachment anxiety",
      "Higher attachment anxiety"
    ),
    aas_anxiety_group = factor(
      aas_anxiety_group,
      levels = c("Lower attachment anxiety", "Higher attachment anxiety")
    ),

    aas_close_group = if_else(
      aas_close_scale <= aas_close_median,
      "Lower closeness discomfort",
      "Higher closeness discomfort"
    ),
    aas_close_group = factor(
      aas_close_group,
      levels = c("Lower closeness discomfort", "Higher closeness discomfort")
    )
  )

# Check final attachment group sizes
study_data %>%
  count(aas_total_group) %>%
  knitr::kable()
aas_total_group n
Lower attachment insecurity 88
Higher attachment insecurity 79

Check Relationship Assessment Scale (RAS) and Adult Attachment Scale (AAS) Reliability

Internal consistency was estimated for the Relationship Assessment Scale, Adult Attachment Scale, Overall Insecurity, Dependence Insecurity, Attachment Anxiety, and Closeness Discomfort scales before the scale scores were used in the primary analyses.

Show code 
# Create item-only data frames for each multi-item rating scale
ras_item_df <- study_data %>% 
  select(all_of(ras_items))

aas_total_item_df <- study_data %>% 
  select(all_of(aas_total_items))

aas_depend_item_df <- study_data %>% 
  select(all_of(aas_depend_items))

aas_anxiety_item_df <- study_data %>% 
  select(all_of(aas_anxiety_items))

aas_close_item_df <- study_data %>% 
  select(all_of(aas_close_items))

# Compute internal consistency estimates
ras_alpha <- psych::alpha(ras_item_df)
ras_omega <- psych::omega(ras_item_df, plot = FALSE)

aas_total_alpha <- psych::alpha(aas_total_item_df)
Some items ( AAS11 ) were negatively correlated with the first principal component and 
probably should be reversed.  
To do this, run the function again with the 'check.keys=TRUE' option
Show code 
aas_total_omega <- psych::omega(aas_total_item_df, plot = FALSE)

aas_depend_alpha <- psych::alpha(aas_depend_item_df)
aas_depend_omega <- psych::omega(aas_depend_item_df, plot = FALSE)

aas_anxiety_alpha <- psych::alpha(aas_anxiety_item_df)
aas_anxiety_omega <- psych::omega(aas_anxiety_item_df, plot = FALSE)

aas_close_alpha <- psych::alpha(aas_close_item_df)
aas_close_omega <- psych::omega(aas_close_item_df, plot = FALSE)

# Print only alpha and omega coefficients
tibble(
  scale = c(
    "Relationship Assessment Scale",
    "AAS Overall Insecurity",
    "AAS Dependence Insecurity",
    "AAS Attachment Anxiety",
    "AAS Closeness Discomfort"
  ),
  alpha = c(
    ras_alpha$total$raw_alpha,
    aas_total_alpha$total$raw_alpha,
    aas_depend_alpha$total$raw_alpha,
    aas_anxiety_alpha$total$raw_alpha,
    aas_close_alpha$total$raw_alpha
  ),
  omega = c(
    ras_omega$omega.tot,
    aas_total_omega$omega.tot,
    aas_depend_omega$omega.tot,
    aas_anxiety_omega$omega.tot,
    aas_close_omega$omega.tot
  )
) %>%

Primary Analyses

This section reports the primary analyses used to test whether communication responsiveness, prior relationship, attachment style, and their interactions predicted relationship satisfaction.

Five 2 x 2 ANOVA models were estimated, with communication responsiveness as the manipulated independent variable and prior relationship experience and attachment style as the categorical moderators.

Model 1: Communication Responsiveness × Prior Relationship Experience

A 2 x 2 ANOVA tested whether relationship satisfaction differed by communication responsiveness, prior relationship experience, and the communication responsiveness x prior relationship experience interaction.

Show code 
a1_ras_relationship <- afex::aov_ez(
  id = "id",
  dv = "ras_scale",
  between = c("condition", "relationship_exp"),
  data = study_data
)

a1_ras_relationship
Anova Table (Type 3 tests)

Response: ras_scale
                      Effect     df  MSE          F  ges p.value
1                  condition 1, 162 0.61 102.10 *** .387   <.001
2           relationship_exp 1, 162 0.61       0.47 .003    .495
3 condition:relationship_exp 1, 162 0.61       1.62 .010    .205
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '+' 0.1 ' ' 1

The ANOVA table reports the main effects of communication responsiveness condition and relationship experience, and the interaction between communication responsiveness and prior relationship experience, for relationship satisfaction scores.

Figures

This section displays the primary 2 x 2 ANOVA results for the five models in figures based on the estimated cell means.

Relationship Satisfaction with Prior Relationship Experience Interaction Plot

Show code 
p_ras_relationship_bar <- ggplot(
  as.data.frame(emmeans(a1_ras_relationship, ~ condition * relationship_exp)),
  aes(
    x = condition,
    y = emmean,
    fill = relationship_exp
  )
) +
  geom_col(
    position = position_dodge(width = 0.65),
    width = 0.55,
    color = "white"
  ) +
  geom_errorbar(
    aes(
      ymin = lower.CL,
      ymax = upper.CL
    ),
    position = position_dodge(width = 0.65),
    width = 0.12,
    linewidth = 0.7
  ) +
  labs(
    x = "Communication Responsiveness Condition",
    y = "Mean Relationship Satisfaction Score",
    fill = "Relationship Experience"
  ) +
  scale_fill_manual(
    values = c(
      "No" = "#C05780",   # YOU CAN CHANGE THESE TWO HEX VALUES TO MATCH YOUR POSTER!
      "Yes" = "#6C88C4"
    )
  ) +
  scale_y_continuous(
    breaks = seq(1, 5, 1)
  ) +
  coord_cartesian(
    ylim = c(1, 5)
  ) +
  theme_classic(
    base_size = 14
  )

p_ras_relationship_bar

The figure shows estimated relationship satisfaction scores by communication responsiveness condition and relationship experience group, with error bars representing 95% confidence intervals.

Results Summary

The primary analyses tested whether communication responsiveness conditions, prior relationship experience group, attachment styles group, and their interaction predicted relationship satisfaction scores. Across the five 2 x2 ANOVA models, communication responsiveness condition, overall attachment insecurity, and dependence insecurity were the only statistically significant predictors. Participants in the high communication responsiveness condition, low attachment insecurity, and lower dependence insecurity reported higher relationship satisfaction scores than participants in the low communication responsiveness condition, high attachment insecurity, and higher dependence insecurity group.

The Prior Relationship Experience, Attachment Anxiety, and Closeness Discomfort groups were not statistically significant predictors of relationship satisfaction. The interaction between the communication responsiveness condition and prior relationship experience group was also not statistically significant for relationship satisfaction, indicating that the difference between high and low communication responsiveness conditions did not meaningfully vary across prior relationship experience groups.

Next, the interaction between communication responsiveness and overall attachment insecurity was also not statistically significant for relationship satisfaction, indicating that the difference between high and low communication responsiveness conditions did not meaningfully vary across overall attachment insecurity groups.

Secondly, the interaction between communication responsiveness and dependence insecurity was also not statistically significant for relationship satisfaction, indicating that the difference between high and low communication responsiveness conditions did not meaningfully vary across dependence insecurity groups.

Therefore, the interaction between communication responsiveness and attachment anxiety was also not statistically significant for relationship satisfaction, indicating that the difference between high and low communication responsiveness conditions did not meaningfully vary across attachment anxiety groups. The estimated means and interaction plots above provide the full model output and visualize the pattern of results for communication responsiveness, prior relationship experience, relationship satisfaction, and attachment style groups.

## About This Report

This reproducible analysis report demonstrates the data preparation, variable construction, descriptive statistics, primary analyses, and figures for the study. 

Therefore, it illustrates how the analyses were produced from the data set using a transparent, reproducible Quarto workflow, examining experiences in long-distance romantic relationships in relation to attachment styles and prior relationship experience. 

## Study Overview

This design study examined whether relationship satisfaction varies with communication responsiveness, prior relationship experience, attachment styles, and their interactions.

The design included one manipulated independent variable and two categorical moderators: Communication Responsiveness (High vs. Low) is the independent variable, and Prior Relationship Experience (Prior vs. None) and Attachment Styles (Secure vs. Insecure) are the moderators. While, the dependent variable was relationship satisfaction. 

Primary analyses tested whether communication responsiveness, prior relationship experience, and attachment styles and their interaction predicted each outcome.

## Setup and Software Environment

This section shows how the packages were installed and downloaded, and how they were used for data preparation, scale construction, statistical modeling, estimation of marginal means, and figure creation. 

**Load Packages**

```{r}

#| warning: false

library(tidyverse)  # data manipulation + plotting
library(psych)      # scale construction + reliability
library(afex)       # ANOVA models + effect sizes
```

## Data Source and Long-Distance Romantic Relationship Analysis Dataset

The data set was imported from the Long Distance Final Project folder, and saved as study_raw so that the original file remained unchanged throughout the report.

Along with this, a smaller analysis data set was then created for the current analyses. The data set contained the study condition variables, demographic variables, relationship assessment items, adult assessment items, dependence items, closeness discomfort items, and anxiety items needed for variable preparation and analysis.

## Variable Preparation

This section prepares the variables used in the primary analyses, with the original imported dataset remaining unchanged, including the prepared variables created in the dataset, study_data. 

------------------------------------------------------------------------

### Prepare Participant ID and Experimental Condition

```{r}
#| label: prepare_id_and_condition
#| echo: true
#| warning: false
#| message: false

study_data <- study_data %>%
  mutate(
    id = row_number(),

    condition = factor(
      condition,
      levels = c(0, 1),
      labels = c("Low", "High")
    ),

    relationship_exp = factor(
      relationship_exp,
      levels = c(0, 1),
      labels = c("No", "Yes")
    ),

    gender = factor(
      gender,
      levels = c(1, 2, 3, 4, 5),
      labels = c(
        "Female",
        "Male",
        "Transgender",
        "Prefer not to say",
        "Other"
      )
    )
  )
```

The experimental condition variables were recoded as a labeled factor for Condition, Relationship Experience, and Gender, resulting in two to five levels for each. Condition and Relationship Experience both have two levels: Low/High and No/Yes. Gender includes five levels: Female, Male, Transgender, Prefer not to say, and Others. As a result, a participant ID variable was created to ensure each row in the analysis dataset had a unique identifier.

```{r}
study_data %>%
```

### Reverse-Code Scale Items

Reverse-Code Scale Items were transformed before Relationship Assessment Scale and Adult Attachment Scale scores were computed. The items used a 1-5 response scale, with reverse coding created by subtracting each original item response from 6. 

```{r}
#| label: reverse_code_items
#| echo: true
#| warning: false
#| message: false

study_data <- study_data %>%
  mutate(
    # Reverse-code RAS items
    # Original scale: 1 to 5
    # Higher recoded scores = higher relationship satisfaction
    RAS4r = 6 - RAS4,
    RAS7r = 6 - RAS7,

    # Reverse-code AAS items
    # Original scale: 1 to 5
    # Higher recoded scores = higher attachment dimension score
    AAS3r  = 6 - AAS3,
    AAS4r  = 6 - AAS4,
    AAS7r  = 6 - AAS7,
    AAS13r = 6 - AAS13,
    AAS14r = 6 - AAS14,
    AAS17r = 6 - AAS17
  )
```

### Check Reverse Coding

```{r}
#| label: check_reverse_coded_items
#| echo: true
#| warning: false
#| message: false

study_data %>%
  select(RAS4, RAS4r, RAS7, RAS7r, AAS3, AAS3r, AAS7, AAS7r) %>%
  head(10) %>%
  knitr::kable()
```

### Create Scale Scores

The reverse-coding scale shows examples of original and reverse-coded items, where the reverse-coded variables were created before the Relationship Assessment Scale and Adult Attachment Scale were computed. 

```{r}
#| label: create_scale_scores
#| echo: true
#| warning: false
#| message: false

ras_items <- c("RAS1", "RAS2", "RAS3", "RAS4r", "RAS5", "RAS6", "RAS7r")

aas_total_items <- c("AAS1", "AAS2", "AAS3r", "AAS4r", "AAS5", 
                     "AAS6", "AAS7r", "AAS8", "AAS9", "AAS10", 
                     "AAS11", "AAS12", "AAS13r", "AAS14r", "AAS15", 
                     "AAS16", "AAS17r", "AAS18")

aas_depend_items <- c("AAS1", "AAS2", "AAS3r", "AAS4r", "AAS5", "AAS6")

aas_anxiety_items <- c("AAS7r", "AAS8", "AAS9", "AAS10", "AAS11", "AAS12")

aas_close_items <- c("AAS13r", "AAS14r", "AAS15", "AAS16", "AAS17r", "AAS18")

study_data <- study_data %>%
  mutate(
    ras_scale = rowMeans(select(., all_of(ras_items)), na.rm = TRUE),
    aas_total_scale = rowMeans(select(., all_of(aas_total_items)), na.rm = TRUE),
    aas_depend_scale = rowMeans(select(., all_of(aas_depend_items)), na.rm = TRUE),
    aas_anxiety_scale = rowMeans(select(., all_of(aas_anxiety_items)), na.rm = TRUE),
    aas_close_scale = rowMeans(select(., all_of(aas_close_items)), na.rm = TRUE)
  )
```

### Check Scale Scores

```{r}
#| label: check_scale_scores
#| echo: true
#| warning: false
#| message: false

study_data %>%
  select(
    ras_scale,
    aas_total_scale,
    aas_depend_scale,
    aas_anxiety_scale,
    aas_close_scale
  ) %>%
  summary()

study_data %>%
  summarise(
    ras_scale_missing = mean(is.na(ras_scale)),
    aas_total_scale_missing = mean(is.na(aas_total_scale)),
    aas_depend_scale_missing = mean(is.na(aas_depend_scale)),
    aas_anxiety_scale_missing = mean(is.na(aas_anxiety_scale)),
    aas_close_scale_missing = mean(is.na(aas_close_scale))
  ) %>%
  knitr::kable()
```

Scale-score checks confirm that computed scale scores for the Relationship Assessment Scale and Adult Attachment Scale are within the expected response range. These also indicate whether any scale scores are missing for overall attachment, dependence, closeness discomfort, or attachment anxiety.

### Create Attachment Groups

Closeness discomfort, dependence, attachment anxiety, and overall attachment group variables were created for the planned 2 x 2 ANOVA models. Participants with attachment scores at or below the sample median were assigned to the Low group, and the participants above the sample median were assigned to the High group.

```{r}
#| label: create_attachment_groups
#| echo: true
#| warning: false
#| message: false

# Create median values for the attachment scale scores
aas_total_median <- median(study_data$aas_total_scale, na.rm = TRUE)
aas_depend_median <- median(study_data$aas_depend_scale, na.rm = TRUE)
aas_anxiety_median <- median(study_data$aas_anxiety_scale, na.rm = TRUE)
aas_close_median <- median(study_data$aas_close_scale, na.rm = TRUE)

# Create median-split attachment groups
study_data <- study_data %>%
  mutate(
    aas_total_group = if_else(
      aas_total_scale <= aas_total_median,
      "Lower attachment insecurity",
      "Higher attachment insecurity"
    ),
    aas_total_group = factor(
      aas_total_group,
      levels = c("Lower attachment insecurity", "Higher attachment insecurity")
    ),

    aas_depend_group = if_else(
      aas_depend_scale <= aas_depend_median,
      "Lower dependence insecurity",
      "Higher dependence insecurity"
    ),
    aas_depend_group = factor(
      aas_depend_group,
      levels = c("Lower dependence insecurity", "Higher dependence insecurity")
    ),

    aas_anxiety_group = if_else(
      aas_anxiety_scale <= aas_anxiety_median,
      "Lower attachment anxiety",
      "Higher attachment anxiety"
    ),
    aas_anxiety_group = factor(
      aas_anxiety_group,
      levels = c("Lower attachment anxiety", "Higher attachment anxiety")
    ),

    aas_close_group = if_else(
      aas_close_scale <= aas_close_median,
      "Lower closeness discomfort",
      "Higher closeness discomfort"
    ),
    aas_close_group = factor(
      aas_close_group,
      levels = c("Lower closeness discomfort", "Higher closeness discomfort")
    )
  )

# Check final attachment group sizes
study_data %>%
  count(aas_total_group) %>%
  knitr::kable()

study_data %>%
  count(aas_depend_group) %>%
  knitr::kable()

study_data %>%
  count(aas_anxiety_group) %>%
  knitr::kable()

study_data %>%
  count(aas_close_group) %>%
  knitr::kable()
```

The median split created the adult attachment grouping variable used in the primary ANOVA models. The output reports the median value used for the split and the number of participants assigned to each attachment style group.

### Check Relationship Assessment Scale (RAS) and Adult Attachment Scale (AAS) Reliability

Internal consistency was estimated for the Relationship Assessment Scale, Adult Attachment Scale, Overall Insecurity, Dependence Insecurity, Attachment Anxiety, and Closeness Discomfort scales before the scale scores were used in the primary analyses.

```{r}
#| label: check_scale_reliability
#| echo: true
#| warning: false
#| message: false

# Create item-only data frames for each multi-item rating scale
ras_item_df <- study_data %>% 
  select(all_of(ras_items))

aas_total_item_df <- study_data %>% 
  select(all_of(aas_total_items))

aas_depend_item_df <- study_data %>% 
  select(all_of(aas_depend_items))

aas_anxiety_item_df <- study_data %>% 
  select(all_of(aas_anxiety_items))

aas_close_item_df <- study_data %>% 
  select(all_of(aas_close_items))

# Compute internal consistency estimates
ras_alpha <- psych::alpha(ras_item_df)
ras_omega <- psych::omega(ras_item_df, plot = FALSE)

aas_total_alpha <- psych::alpha(aas_total_item_df)
aas_total_omega <- psych::omega(aas_total_item_df, plot = FALSE)

aas_depend_alpha <- psych::alpha(aas_depend_item_df)
aas_depend_omega <- psych::omega(aas_depend_item_df, plot = FALSE)

aas_anxiety_alpha <- psych::alpha(aas_anxiety_item_df)
aas_anxiety_omega <- psych::omega(aas_anxiety_item_df, plot = FALSE)

aas_close_alpha <- psych::alpha(aas_close_item_df)
aas_close_omega <- psych::omega(aas_close_item_df, plot = FALSE)

# Print only alpha and omega coefficients
tibble(
  scale = c(
    "Relationship Assessment Scale",
    "AAS Overall Insecurity",
    "AAS Dependence Insecurity",
    "AAS Attachment Anxiety",
    "AAS Closeness Discomfort"
  ),
  alpha = c(
    ras_alpha$total$raw_alpha,
    aas_total_alpha$total$raw_alpha,
    aas_depend_alpha$total$raw_alpha,
    aas_anxiety_alpha$total$raw_alpha,
    aas_close_alpha$total$raw_alpha
  ),
  omega = c(
    ras_omega$omega.tot,
    aas_total_omega$omega.tot,
    aas_depend_omega$omega.tot,
    aas_anxiety_omega$omega.tot,
    aas_close_omega$omega.tot
  )
) %>%
  knitr::kable(digits = 2)
```

In the reliability table, Cronbach’s alpha and McDonald’s omega were reported for the Relationship Assessment Scale and the Adult Attachment Scale in this reproducible analysis report.

## Primary Analyses

This section reports the primary analyses used to test whether communication responsiveness, prior relationship, attachment style, and their interactions predicted relationship satisfaction.

Five 2 x 2 ANOVA models were estimated, with communication responsiveness as the manipulated independent variable and prior relationship experience and attachment style as the categorical moderators.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

### **Model 1:** Communication Responsiveness × Prior Relationship Experience

A 2 x 2 ANOVA tested whether relationship satisfaction differed by communication responsiveness, prior relationship experience, and the communication responsiveness x prior relationship experience interaction.

```{r}
#| label: anova_ras_relationship
#| echo: true
#| warning: false
#| message: false

a1_ras_relationship <- afex::aov_ez(
  id = "id",
  dv = "ras_scale",
  between = c("condition", "relationship_exp"),
  data = study_data
)

a1_ras_relationship
```

The ANOVA table reports the main effects of communication responsiveness condition and relationship experience, and the interaction between communication responsiveness and prior relationship experience, for relationship satisfaction scores.

### Estimated Means for Communication Responsiveness × Prior Relationship Experience

```{r}
#| label: estimated_means_ras_relationship
#| echo: true
#| warning: false
#| message: false

emmeans::emmeans(a1_ras_relationship, ~ condition)

emmeans::emmeans(a1_ras_relationship, ~ relationship_exp)

emmeans::emmeans(a1_ras_relationship, ~ condition * relationship_exp)
```

The estimated means show the pattern of relationship satisfaction scores across the communication responsiveness condition, prior relationship experience, and their combined cells.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Figures

This section displays the primary 2 x 2 ANOVA results for the five models in figures based on the estimated cell means. 

### Relationship Satisfaction with Prior Relationship Experience Interaction Plot

```{r}
#| label: ras_relationship_interaction_plot
#| echo: true
#| warning: false
#| message: false

p_ras_relationship_bar <- ggplot(
  as.data.frame(emmeans(a1_ras_relationship, ~ condition * relationship_exp)),
  aes(
    x = condition,
    y = emmean,
    fill = relationship_exp
  )
) +
  geom_col(
    position = position_dodge(width = 0.65),
    width = 0.55,
    color = "white"
  ) +
  geom_errorbar(
    aes(
      ymin = lower.CL,
      ymax = upper.CL
    ),
    position = position_dodge(width = 0.65),
    width = 0.12,
    linewidth = 0.7
  ) +
  labs(
    x = "Communication Responsiveness Condition",
    y = "Mean Relationship Satisfaction Score",
    fill = "Relationship Experience"
  ) +
  scale_fill_manual(
    values = c(
      "No" = "#C05780",   # YOU CAN CHANGE THESE TWO HEX VALUES TO MATCH YOUR POSTER!
      "Yes" = "#6C88C4"
    )
  ) +
  scale_y_continuous(
    breaks = seq(1, 5, 1)
  ) +
  coord_cartesian(
    ylim = c(1, 5)
  ) +
  theme_classic(
    base_size = 14
  )

p_ras_relationship_bar
```

The figure shows estimated relationship satisfaction scores by communication responsiveness condition and relationship experience group, with error bars representing 95% confidence intervals.

```{r}
  geom_col(
    position = position_dodge(width = 0.65),
    width = 0.55,
    color = "white"
  ) +
  geom_errorbar(
    aes(
      ymin = lower.CL,
      ymax = upper.CL
    ),
    position = position_dodge(width = 0.65),
    width = 0.12,
    linewidth = 0.7
  ) +
  labs(
    x = "Communication Responsiveness Condition",
    y = "Mean Relationship Satisfaction Score",
    fill = "Overall Attachment Insecurity"
  ) +
  scale_fill_manual(
    values = c(
      "Lower attachment insecurity" = "#C05780",   # YOU CAN CHANGE THESE TWO HEX VALUES TO MATCH YOUR POSTER!
      "Higher attachment insecurity" = "#6C88C4"
    )
  ) +
  scale_y_continuous(
    breaks = seq(1, 5, 1)
  ) +
  coord_cartesian(
    ylim = c(1, 5)
  ) +
  theme_classic(
    base_size = 14
  )

p_ras_aas_total_bar
```

The figure shows estimated relationship satisfaction scores by communication responsiveness condition and overall attachment insecurity group, with error bars representing 95% confidence intervals.

## Results Summary

The primary analyses tested whether communication responsiveness conditions, prior relationship experience group, attachment styles group, and their interaction predicted relationship satisfaction scores. Across the five 2 x2 ANOVA models, communication responsiveness condition, overall attachment insecurity, and dependence insecurity were the only statistically significant predictors. Participants in the high communication responsiveness condition, low attachment insecurity, and lower dependence insecurity reported higher relationship satisfaction scores than participants in the low communication responsiveness condition, high attachment insecurity, and higher dependence insecurity group. 

The Prior Relationship Experience, Attachment Anxiety, and Closeness Discomfort groups were not statistically significant predictors of relationship satisfaction. The interaction between the communication responsiveness condition and prior relationship experience group was also not statistically significant for relationship satisfaction, indicating that the difference between high and low communication responsiveness conditions did not meaningfully vary across prior relationship experience groups. 

Next, the interaction between communication responsiveness and overall attachment insecurity was also not statistically significant for relationship satisfaction, indicating that the difference between high and low communication responsiveness conditions did not meaningfully vary across overall attachment insecurity groups. 

Secondly, the interaction between communication responsiveness and dependence insecurity was also not statistically significant for relationship satisfaction, indicating that the difference between high and low communication responsiveness conditions did not meaningfully vary across dependence insecurity groups. 

Therefore, the interaction between communication responsiveness and attachment anxiety was also not statistically significant for relationship satisfaction, indicating that the difference between high and low communication responsiveness conditions did not meaningfully vary across attachment anxiety groups. The estimated means and interaction plots above provide the full model output and visualize the pattern of results for communication responsiveness, prior relationship experience, relationship satisfaction, and attachment style groups.
